Besides the obvious variables of title, genre, director, year, and duration, the rest of the variables are as follows:

  • gross : The gross earnings in the US box office, not adjusted for inflation

  • budget: The movie's budget

  • cast_facebook_likes: the number of facebook likes cast memebrs received

  • votes: the number of people who voted for (or rated) the movie in IMDB

  • reviews: the number of reviews for that movie

  • rating: IMDB average rating

Average gross, budget, and return on budget by genre¶

Produce a table with the average gross earning and budget (gross and budget) by genre. Calculate a variable return_on_budget which shows how many dollars did a movie make at the box office for each dollar of its budget. Rank genres by this return_on_budget in descending order.

In [7]:
# Average gross, budget, and return on budget by genre

# Group once, take the two means, then derive return_on_budget inside .assign()
# so the whole calculation reads as a single top-to-bottom chain.
return_by_genre = (
    movies
    .groupby("genre")
    .agg(mean_gross=("gross", "mean"),
         mean_budget=("budget", "mean"))
    .assign(return_on_budget=lambda d: d["mean_gross"] / d["mean_budget"])
    .sort_values("return_on_budget", ascending=False)
    .round(2)
    .reset_index()
)

Top 15 directors by gross revenue¶

Produce a table that shows the top 15 directors who have created the highest gross revenue in the box office. Don't just show the total gross amount, but also the mean, median, and standard deviation per director.

# Top 15 directors by gross revenue

# A single groupby with named aggregations produces every statistic in one pass;
# sort by total gross and keep the 15 biggest earners.
top_directors = (
    movies
    .groupby("director")
    .agg(total_gross=("gross", "sum"),
         mean_gross=("gross", "mean"),
         median_gross=("gross", "median"),
         std_gross=("gross", "std"))
    .sort_values("total_gross", ascending=False)
    .head(15)
    .round(0)
    .reset_index()
)

Use seaborn to answer the following:¶

Gross vs. cast Facebook likes¶

  • Examine the relationship between gross and cast_facebook_likes. Produce a scatterplot and write one sentence discussing whether the number of facebook likes that the cast has received is likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office. What variable are you going to map to the Y- and X- axes?

Answer: With a correlation of only about 0.21, cast Facebook likes are a weak predictor of gross — the points form a very diffuse cloud and plenty of low-popularity casts still produced high-grossing films — so on their own they would make a poor predictor of box-office revenue. (Gross → Y axis, cast_facebook_likes → X axis, since gross is the outcome we are trying to explain.)

In [9]:
# Scatter plot: Gross vs Cast Facebook Likes

# Predictor (cast_facebook_likes) on X, outcome (gross) on Y: we ask whether more
# cast popularity is associated with higher box-office takings.
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

# regplot draws the scatter, fits a linear regression line, and shades its 95% CI.
sns.regplot(
    data=movies,
    x="cast_facebook_likes",
    y="gross",
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.3},    # fade points so dense regions stay readable
    line_kws={"color": "crimson"},
)

plt.title("Gross vs. Cast Facebook Likes")
plt.xlabel("Cast Facebook likes")
plt.ylabel("Gross (US box office, $)")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Pearson correlation quantifies the (weak) linear association shown above.
correlation = movies["gross"].corr(movies["cast_facebook_likes"])
print(f"Correlation between gross and cast facebook likes: {correlation:.3f}")

Correlation between gross and cast facebook likes: 0.213

Gross vs. budget¶

  • Examine the relationship between gross and budget. Produce a scatterplot and write one sentence discussing whether budget is likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office.

Answer: Budget shows a clear positive relationship with gross (correlation ≈ 0.64): bigger budgets tend to bring bigger box-office takings, so budget is a reasonably good — though far from perfect — predictor of gross.

In [10]:
# Scatter plot: Gross vs Budget

# Budget on X, gross on Y — does spending more tend to earn more at the box office?
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

sns.regplot(
    data=movies,
    x="budget",
    y="gross",
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.3},
    line_kws={"color": "crimson"},
)

plt.title("Gross vs. Budget")
plt.xlabel("Budget ($)")
plt.ylabel("Gross (US box office, $)")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Correlation between gross and budget: "
      f"{movies['gross'].corr(movies['budget']):.3f}")

Correlation between gross and budget: 0.641

Gross vs. rating, faceted by genre¶

  • Examine the relationship between gross and rating. Produce a scatterplot, faceted by genre and discuss whether IMDB ratings are likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office. Is there anything strange in this dataset?

Answer: Within essentially every genre the relationship between IMDB rating and gross is weak and roughly flat, so ratings are a poor predictor of box-office revenue. The strange feature is exactly that flatness — some of the highest-grossing films have only middling ratings — and a few thinly-populated genres show almost no pattern at all, which is why we restrict the facets to genres with at least 5 films.

In [11]:
# Scatter plot: Gross vs Rating by Genre- for genres that have at least 5 movies

# Reuse the ">=5 films" filter so sparse genres don't create near-empty facets.
counts = movies["genre"].value_counts()
movies_big = movies[movies["genre"].isin(counts[counts >= 5].index)]

# lmplot = scatter + fitted regression line, one facet per genre.
g = sns.lmplot(
    data=movies_big,
    x="rating",
    y="gross",
    col="genre",
    col_wrap=4,
    height=2.5,
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.3},
    facet_kws={"sharey": False},
)
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.set_axis_labels("IMDB rating", "Gross ($)")
g.fig.suptitle("Gross vs. IMDB rating by genre (genres with ≥5 films)", y=1.02)

Returns of financial stocks¶

You may find useful the material on finance data sources.

We will use the yfinance package to download historical data of stock prices, calculate returns, and examine the distribution of returns.

We must first identify which stocks we want to download data for, and for this we must know their ticker symbol; Apple is known as AAPL, Microsoft as MSFT, McDonald's as MCD, etc. The file nyse.csv contains 508 stocks listed on the NYSE, their ticker symbol, name, the IPO (Initial Public Offering) year, and the sector and industry the company is in.

Choose stocks and download data¶

Next, let's choose some stocks and their ticker symbols and download some data. You MUST choose 6 different stocks from the ones listed below; You should, however, add SPY which is the SP500 ETF (Exchange Traded Fund).

In [12]:
# Download stock data

# The 6 chosen stocks plus SPY (the S&P 500 ETF)
my_stocks = ["AAPL", "JPM", "DIS", "DPZ", "ANF", "XOM", "SPY"]

# Date range: start on 1 January five years ago, end today.
# Computed from today's date so it always stays current when re-run.
end_date = pd.Timestamp.today().normalize()
start_date = pd.Timestamp(year=end_date.year - 5, month=1, day=1)

# Download every ticker in ONE call. Passing a list to yf.download returns a
# frame with a two-level column index (field, ticker); selecting "Adj Close"
# collapses it to a tidy price matrix: dates on the index, one column per stock.
prices = yf.download(
    my_stocks,
    start=start_date,
    end=end_date,
    auto_adjust=False,   # keep the explicit "Adj Close" column
    progress=False,
)["Adj Close"]

# yfinance returns the columns alphabetically, so reorder to match our list.
prices = prices[my_stocks]

print(f"Downloaded {start_date.date()} to {end_date.date()}")
print("Adjusted-close price matrix:", prices.shape)   # (trading days, stocks)
prices.head()

Calculate daily and monthly returns¶

Financial performance analysis depend on returns; If I buy a stock today for 100 and I sell it tomorrow for 101.75, my one-day return, assuming no transaction costs, is 1.75%. So given the adjusted closing prices, our first step is to calculate daily and monthly returns.

In [13]:
# Calculate returns

# pct_change() on the whole DataFrame computes returns for every stock at once.
daily_returns = prices.pct_change()

# Resample to month-end ("ME") / year-end ("YE"), take the last price in each
# period, then compute the percentage change. (Older pandas uses "M" / "Y".)
monthly_returns = prices.resample("ME").last().pct_change()
yearly_returns  = prices.resample("YE").last().pct_change()

Density plot of monthly returns¶

Plot a density plot, using sns.kdeplot(), for each of the stocks

In [16]:
# Density plot of monthly returns

# Reshape to long ("tidy") form so seaborn can colour by stock with `hue`:
# one row per (date, stock, monthly_return).
monthly_long = (
    monthly_returns
    .melt(value_name="monthly_return", var_name="stock", ignore_index=False)
    .dropna()
)

sns.set_style("whitegrid")

# displot draws every stock's KDE on a single seaborn figure, no manual loop.
g = sns.displot(
    data=monthly_long,
    x="monthly_return",
    hue="stock",
    kind="kde",
    fill=True,
    alpha=0.3,
    height=6,
    aspect=1.5,
)
g.set_axis_labels("Monthly Return", "Density")
g.fig.suptitle("Density of Monthly Returns by Stock", y=1.02)
Out[16]:
Text(0.5, 1.02, 'Density of Monthly Returns by Stock')

What can you infer from this plot? Which stock is the riskiest? The least risky?

TYPE YOUR ANSWER AFTER (AND OUTSIDE!) THIS BLOCKQUOTE.

The width of each density curve reflects volatility. ANF has by far the widest, flattest distribution (monthly SD ≈ 16.8%), which makes it the riskiest stock. SPY — the diversified S&P 500 ETF — has the tallest, narrowest curve (SD ≈ 4.4%), which makes it the least risky. This is what we'd expect: a single fashion retailer swings far more than a basket of 500 companies.

Risk-return plot¶

Finally, make a plot that shows the expected monthly return (mean) of a stock on the Y axis and the risk (standard deviation) in the X-axis. Please use plt.annotate() to label each stock

In [19]:
# Risk-return plot
# monthly_summary already holds each stock's mean (return) and std (risk),
# so we can plot straight from it. reset_index turns the ticker into a column.
risk_return = monthly_summary.reset_index(names="stock")

sns.set_style("whitegrid")
ax = sns.scatterplot(
    data=risk_return,
    x="std",
    y="mean",
    hue="stock",
    s=150,
    legend=False,
)

# Label each point, one annotation per row.
for row in risk_return.itertuples():
    ax.annotate(row.stock, (row.std, row.mean),
                xytext=(6, 4), textcoords="offset points")

ax.set(
    xlabel="Risk (Standard Deviation of Monthly Returns)",
    ylabel="Expected Monthly Return (Mean)",
    title="Risk-Return Profile of Stocks",
)

# Format both axes as percentages with one decimal (values are decimals, so xmax=1).
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(xmax=1, decimals=1))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(xmax=1, decimals=1))

What can you infer from this plot? Are there any stocks which, while being riskier, do not have a higher expected return?

TYPE YOUR ANSWER AFTER (AND OUTSIDE!) THIS BLOCKQUOTE

Yes. DIS and DPZ sit to the right of AAPL, JPM and XOM (higher standard deviation) yet lower on the return axis — DIS actually posts a slightly negative mean monthly return despite being one of the most volatile names, so both took on extra risk without being compensated for it. At the other extreme, ANF is the riskiest name but also the highest-returning, while SPY delivers a solid return at the lowest risk — a neat illustration of the diversification benefit of holding the index rather than a single stock.

Rents in San Francisco 2000-2018¶

Kate Pennington created a panel of historic Craigslist rents by scraping posts archived by the Wayback Machine. You can read more about her work here:

What impact does new housing have on rents, displacement, and gentrification in the surrounding neighborhood? Read our interview with economist Kate Pennington about her article, "Does Building New Housing Cause Displacement?:The Supply and Demand Effects of Construction in San Francisco."

In our case, we have a clean(ish) dataset with about 200K rows that correspond to Craigslist listings for renting properties in the greater SF area. The data dictionary is as follows:

Variable types and missing values¶

What are the variable types? Do they all correspond to what they really are? Which variables have most missing values?

Answer: Most columns are typed sensibly — price, beds, baths, sqft, lat, lon are numeric and the text fields are objects. The main mismatch is date, stored as an integer (YYYYMMDD) rather than a true datetime, while year is a number that really behaves as a category. The columns with the most missing values are the free-text and geolocation fields — descr, address, lon, lat, details — followed by baths and sqft; the core fields such as price, city and year are essentially complete.

In [15]:
# Data inspection

# Calculating the total no. of missing values in each column of the dataset,
# sorted so the worst offenders are at the top (with a % for context).
missing = (
    rent.isna().sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .rename("n_missing")
    .to_frame()
    .assign(pct_missing=lambda d: (d["n_missing"] / len(rent) * 100).round(1))
)

Top 20 cities by % of listings¶

Make a plot that shows the top 20 cities in terms of % of classifieds between 2000-2018. You need to calculate the number of listings by city, and then convert that number to a %.

The final graph should look like this:

In [ ]:
# Top 20 cities by percentage of listings

# Share of all listings held by each city (as a %), keeping the 20 largest.
top20_cities = (
    rent["city"]
    .value_counts()
    #.value_counts(normalize=True)
    .reset_index(name="n_listings")
    .assign(pct_listings=lambda d: d["n_listings"] / d["n_listings"].sum() * 100)
    .rename(columns={"index": "city"})
    .head(20)
)

top20_cities = (
    rent
    .groupby("city")
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="n_listings")
    .assign(pct_listings=lambda d: d["n_listings"] / d["n_listings"].sum() * 100)
    .sort_values("pct_listings", ascending=False)
    .head(20)
)


plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
ax = sns.barplot(data=top20_cities, x="pct_listings", y="city", color="grey")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(decimals=0))  # values already in %
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="")
plt.title("San Francisco accounts for more than a quarter of all rental classifieds\n"
          "% of Craigslist listings, 2000-2018", loc="left")
plt.figtext(0.99, -0.02,
            "Source: Pennington, Kate (2018). Bay Area Craigslist Rental Housing Posts, 2000-2018",
            ha="right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Median prices in San Francisco by bedrooms¶

Make a plot that shows the evolution of median prices in San Francisco for 0, 1, 2, and 3 bedrooms listings. The final graph should resemble this

In [17]:
# Time-series of median rents in San Francisco (0-3 bedrooms)

# Data Prep: keep SF listings for 0-3 beds, then the median price per year and bedroom count.
sf_by_beds = (
    rent
    .query("city == 'san francisco' and beds in [0, 1, 2, 3]")
    .astype({"beds": "int"})          # 0.0 -> 0 so the facet titles read cleanly
    .groupby(["year", "beds"], as_index=False)["price"]
    .median()
)

# One facet per bedroom count, each its own coloured line (matches the target layout).
g = sns.relplot(
    data=sf_by_beds,
    x="year", y="price",
    col="beds", hue="beds",
    kind="line", palette="husl",
    height=3.5, aspect=0.7, legend=False,
)
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.set_axis_labels("", "Median price ($)")
g.fig.suptitle("San Francisco rents have been steadily increasing\n0 to 3-bed listings, 2000-2018",
               y=1.05, x=0.02, ha="left")

Median rents for the top 12 Bay Area cities¶

Finally, make a plot that shows median rental prices for the top 12 cities in the Bay area (for 1 bedroom rentals). Your final graph should look like this

In [18]:
# Median rental prices for top 12 cities (in terms of number of ads) in Bay Area

# The 12 cities with the most listings overall.
top12 = rent["city"].value_counts().head(12).index

# For 1-bedroom flats only, the median price per year in each of those cities.
onebed = (
    rent
    .query("beds == 1 and city in @top12")
    .groupby(["year", "city"], as_index=False)["price"]
    .median()
)

g = sns.relplot(
    data=onebed,
    x="year", y="price",
    col="city", hue="city",
    col_wrap=4, kind="line",
    height=2.2, aspect=1.3, legend=False,
)
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.set_axis_labels("", "Median price ($)")
g.fig.suptitle("Rental prices for 1-bedroom flats in the Bay Area", y=1.02, x=0.02, ha="left")

What can you infer from these plots? Don't just explain what's in the graph, but speculate or tell a short story (1-2 paragraphs max).

TYPE YOUR ANSWER AFTER (AND OUTSIDE!) THIS BLOCKQUOTE.

Across the Bay Area, median rents climb steadily from the early 2000s, wobble around the 2008–09 financial crisis, and then accelerate sharply through the 2010s. San Francisco commands the highest prices and the steepest late rise, with a two- or three-bedroom flat roughly doubling over the period.

The most plausible story is the tech boom: as well-paid engineering jobs flooded into San Francisco and the surrounding cities (Mountain View, Palo Alto, Sunnyvale), demand for housing surged while new construction lagged well behind. With supply effectively fixed in the short run, that extra demand showed up almost entirely as higher rents — and it rippled outward, so even cheaper commuter cities like Union City and Santa Rosa saw prices march upward in the second half of the sample.
